Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellants. 
Not represented ------ The Respondents.
parties:
MA Hashem and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Shafiuddin Ahmed & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos.1 and 2, Government of Bangladesh and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Narayanganj, by filing one set of written statement and by the defendant Nos. 6-8 i.e. the appellants, by filing separate set of written statement. The defendants denied the averments made in the plaint. It is the case of the defendants that the land described' in schedule 'Kha' i.e. accreted land, did not accrete till the publication of the SA record on 1-8-1963, that land described in schedule 'kha' accreted to the CS Plot Nos. 670, 671, 674, 675, 676 and 250 after the publication of the SA record i.e. coming into operation of part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. It is the case of the defendant Nos. 1-2 that in respect of the accreted land to the aforesaid CS plots "চর্চা ম্যাপ" was prepared by the Collector of the Narayanganj Collectorate and the accreted lands to the CS plots were recorded in "চর্চা ম্যাপ". Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 asserted that it is not correct to say that the land described in schedule 'kha' accreted in 1935 or that before 1-8-1963 and that at the time of preparation of SA record and at the time of publication thereof on 1-8-1963 there was no existence of the accreted land as described in schedule 'kha', that the accreted land in respect whereof "চর্চা ম্যাপ" was prepared and listed in plots were given settlement to the defendant Nos. 6-8 in Settlement Case Nos. 265 of 1988-89 and 229 of 1988-89 for the use of industrial purpose, that the land of CS Plot Nos. 670, 671, 674, 675,676 and 250 have been acquired by the Government in LA Case No. 27 of 1978-79 for utilisation by the defendant Nos. 6-8. 

 5. It was the case of the defendant Nos. 6-8 that the land described in schedule 'kha' was the Government's khas land and the said land has been settled with the defendants by starting Settlement Case Nos. 265 and 229 of 1988-89 and the land so taken lease is possessed by them. It is also the case of the defendants that at the time of SA survey which started in 1956 and continued upto some part of 1963 there was no existence of the land described in schedule 'kha' or, in other words, there was no accretion of land as described in schedule 'kha' to the CS plots land whereof has been acquired by the Government in LA Case Nos. 27 of 1978-79, that land described in schedule 'kha' accreted to the CS plots after publication of the SA record on 1-8-1963 i.e. subsequent to the coming into operation of the part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 6. It may be mentioned the plaintiffs are claiming the land in suit by purchase and as heirs of the purchasers and the purchases were made between 1932 and 1968. It was the case of the plaintiffs that land described in schedule 'Kha' accreted in 1935 to the CS Plots. If that assertion of the plaintiffs is accepted then it would have been quite natural to have the mention of the accreted land in the kabalas of the years between 1943 and 1968 and there would have been mention of said fact upon referring to the plot(s) to which there was accretion of land and the quantity thereof, but conspicuously in the deeds of the years 1943-1968 there is no mention of the plot of the accreted land nor quantity of land accreted to particular CS plot and also there is no mention of quantity as stated hereinbefore. It was the definite case of the defendants that there was no existence of accreted land till 1963 i.e. at the time when the SA record was made final. Had there been any accretion of land to the CS plot during SA survey the same would have surely been recorded in the SA record which was published on 1-8-1963. In the aforesaid state of the matter it has been observed by the trial Court that there was no reason to believe that the accreted land was in existence in 1963. It may be mentioned that during the period between 1935-1947 no rent was paid by the plaintiffs in respect of the land said to have accreted to the CS plots. 

 7. The plaintiffs tried to make out a case upon referring to the recital in the deed as to transfer of the land of CS plot with accreted land and asserted that there had been existence of accretal land prior to the coming into operation of part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or, in other words, prior to the publication of the SA record which was finally published on 1-8-1963. The case so tried to make out by the plaintiffs about the existence of accretal land prior to preparation of SA record and at the time of preparation and publication of SA record hardly inspires one to accept the same as correct since had the accretal land been in existence at the time of preparation of the SA records the same surely would have been recorded in the SA Records and that there would have been no occasion for the Government to prepare the "চর্চা ম্যাপ" with "m" plot in respect of the land accreted to the CS plots mentioned hereinbefore. The land of the "চর্চা ম্যাপ" with "চর্চা" plot has been recorded in the name of the Government in khas khatian. 

 13. Leave was granted to consider the contentions whether the High Court Division was wrong in setting aside the finding of the trial Court without adverting to the reasoning assigned by it and upon a completely erroneous view that the trial Court was not aware of the legal position as settled by this Division in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195, whether the High Court Division without applying its judicial mind to the finding of the trial Court and to the oral and documentary evidence on record wrongly set aside the judgment of the trial Court, whether the High Court Division proceeded on the wrong premise that in deciding the suit the trial Court not been aware of the law enunciated in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195, since had the trial Court not been aware of the law settled by this Division in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195, the said Court would not have put emphasis on the question as to whether there has been accretion of the land as claimed by the plaintiffs prior to 1-8-1963 or after 1-8-1963 i.e. after coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, whether payment of rent in respect of the accreted land would have been the best evidence to establish that the land so accreted was recorded in SA khatian and that plaintiffs paid rent in respect of the accreted land, but evidence is nil as to payment of rent at any point of time i.e. the period starting from 1935 as claimed by the plaintiffs. It may be mentioned the plaintiffs have asserted that accretion took place in 1935. Even if it is taken that accretion was not complete in 1935, as the High Court Division considered, but started in 1935 and gradually there has been accretion till the time of their purchase, prior to coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in the year 1944, but the said fact i.e. accretion started in 1935 and that at the time of the purchase made in 1944 there was existence of the accreted land has not been established by the plaintiffs by leading any tangible evidence and that the fact of payment of rent for the accreted land till the time of acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government to the landlord has not been established by adducing any evidence. The undisputed position is that the accreted land has not been recorded in SA khatian. Had the accreted land been in existence since 1935 and at the time of preparation of the SA record and had the plaintiffs any claim in the accreted land they would have certainly got the accreted land recorded in their name in SA khatian. This vital fact shows that at the time of preparation of the SA record the accreted land was not in existence or, in other words, there has been accretion of the land as claimed by the plaintiffs subsequent to the coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and in that state of the matter the Government got the accreted land surveyed and prepared the চর্চা ম্যাপ" with the চর্চা" plot. The learned Counsel further submitted that the trial Court. was not in error in holding in the background of the materials on record that the plaintiffs failed to prove that there has been accretion of the land claimed by them to the CS plot Nos. 670, 671, 674, 675, 676 and 250 as well as the corresponding RS plot Nos. 605, 608, 613, 613, 612 and 302 before coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. As stated hereinbefore Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 came into operation in the Dhaka District on 1-8-1963 vide notification No. SA 116/63/609 dated 18th July, 1963 published in the Dhaka Gazette (ordinary) dated 1st August, 1963 (part 1, page 1169). In the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195 it has been observed, "The date of the commencement of Part V of the Act in any area must necessarily be a date later than that of the publication of the notification under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act in that area ..... only such accretions, as took place after Part V of the Act had come into force in the area where the accreted lands are situated, have been brought under the purview of sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 87 of the Act. It is natural that sub-section (3) will have operation only in respect of such accretions as have been contemplated in sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 87 of the Act. 

 14. We have noticed that all accretions, which took place before the notification under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act, have been statutorily recognised to be the lands appertaining to the tenancies of the riparian owners and the provisions of clause (e) and (f) of section 3(4) or items (2) and (4) of section 44 of the Act have clearly conferred the right of tenancy upon the riparian owner in respect of such accreted lands". 

 15. It is seen from the judgment of the trial Court that the said Court in its judgment in more than one place had put stress on the question relating to time of accretion of the land described in schedule 'kha' in the background of the contention of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and 6-8, and on consideration of the materials on record held that the land in suit i.e. accreted land as claimed by the plaintiffs were not in existence at the time of preparation of the SA record and that on 1-8-1963 when Part V of the Act came into operation in Dhaka District. This clearly shows that the trial Court was quite aware of the proposition of law laid down in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195 that in case of accretion of land prior to the coming into operation of Part V of the Act the tenant to whose land there has been accretion would be the tenant or, in other words, would be the owner of that accreted land, but if there is accretion of land to the tenancy of a person subsequent to the coming into operation of Part V of the Act the land so accreted would remain to the Government. As stated hereinbefore the plaintiffs did not establish by leading any evidence that there has been accretion of the land as claimed by them to their tenancy prior to the coming into operation of Part V of the Act i.e. prior to 1-8- 1963, and that as the claimant of the land paid rent either to the landlord prior to the acquisition of rent receiving interest or to the Government any time prior to the coming into operation of Part V of the Act i.e. on 1-8-1963. 

 16. It has been submitted that the High Court Division proceeded on the wrong premise that the trial Court was unaware of the proposition of law laid down in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195. On perusal of the judgment of the trial Court we are of the view the submission or the contention so made by the learned Counsel of the appellant appears to be of merit. As stated hereinbefore the trial Court while dismissing the suit considered the question of accretion' of the land claimed by the plaintiffs prior to 1-8-1963 and that the fact of accretion of the land prior to 1-8-1963 having not been established the trial Court dismissed the suit amongst others, on this ground also. The plaintiffs filed the suit seeking declaration that the settlement made by the Government to the defendant Nos. 6-8 of the land claimed by them as accreted land was illegal and the proceeding of the LA case was not legal and prayed for recovery of khas possession of 4 decimals of land described in schedule 'ga' to the plaint. It is the plaintiffs' case that they have been dispossessed by the defendants from 4 decimals of land described in schedule 'ga'. This means the plaintiffs are in possession of the rest of the land in suit i.e. 2.91 acres of land. The total land in suit is 2.95 acres. The suit as framed was declaratory suit simpliciter in respect of the land described in schedule 'kha' to the plaint measuring 2.95 acres i.e. the accreted land. The trial Court on consideration of the oral evidence as well as the documentary evidence arrived at the definite finding that the plaintiffs are not in possession of the land described in schedule 'kha' and that failed to establish that they have been dispossessed from the land described in schedule 'ga'. Since the plaintiffs are not in possession of the land in suit and also failed to prove their case of dispossession from the land of 'ga' schedule they are not entitled to the relief as prayed for. The trial Court has held that the land in suit belonged to the Government and the Government settled the same to the defendant Nos. 6-8. The finding of the trial Court as to that the land in suit belonged to the Government has been made upon arriving at the finding that at the time of final publication of SA khatian in 1963 the accreted land was not in existence or, in other words, there has been accretion of the land claimed by the plaintiffs after coming into operation of Part V of the Act and, as such, the same belonged to the Government. The aforesaid finding of the trial Court clearly demonstrates that the said Court was quite aware of the law laid down in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195. This being the position the High Court Division was in error in holding that the trial Court was unaware of law laid down by this Division in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195. From the judgment of the trial Court it is seen that the said Court on detailed discussions and considerations of the evidence, both oral and documentary, arrived at the finding that there has been accretion to the CS plots after coming into operation of Part V of the Act. 

 17. The learned Advocate for the appellants has submitted that a tenant cannot claim accreted land in excess of the land of his original tenancy as per provision in the proviso to the first paragraph of Regulation 4 of the Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation XI of 1825. The proviso to the aforesaid first paragraph of Regulation 4 runs as: 

 "Provided that the increment of land thus obtained shall not entitle the person in possession of the estate or tenure to which the land may be annexed to a right of property or permanent interest therein beyond that possessed by him in the estate or tenure to which the land may be annexed, and shall not in any case be understood to exempt the holder of it from the payment to the Government of any assessment for the public revenue to which it may be liable under the provisions of Regulation II, 1819, or of any other Regulation in force". 

 18. It is seen from the materials on record, at least in two cases, i.e. CS plot Nos. 676 and 250, land accreted and claimed as accreted land is more than the land for which there has been tenancy. The contention so made is not so much relevant for the disposal of the appeal since the point involved in the appeal whether the High Court Division without adverting to the reasoning’s given and findings arrived at by the trial Court in disposing of the suit and the trial Court also having had considered the provision of law as regard accretion after coming into operation of part V of the Act in the particular locality the High Court Division without disposing of the appeal on merit was correct in sending the suit back on remand. 

 20. It is seen from the judgment of the trial Court that the defendants by adducing reliable evidence proved their possession in the entire land in suit. The fact of defendants being in possession of the land in suit has also been admitted by the plaintiffs' witnesses. In that state of the matter the claim of the plaintiffs that they are in possession of the land in suit except 4(four) decimals is anything but not the fact. Had the plaintiffs would have started to claim and to possess the land gradually accreted to the CS plots they would have certainly been in possession, but they failed to prove their claim of possession in the accreted land i.e. land in suit. The Government settled the accreted land with the defendant Nos. 6-8 by starting Settlement Case Nos. 265 and 229 of 1988-89 and made over possession to the said settlement holders on 30-5-1989. As against the settlement so made and possession made over to the defendant Nos. 6-8 by the Government the plaintiffs did not take any step. The defendants have proved the fact of settling the land in suit with them and handing over possession of the land so settled with them by oral and documentary evidence. As stated hereinbefore that the appellate Court did not at all consider legality of the judgment appealed before it. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division has sent back the case on remand to afford an opportunity to the parties to, adduce evidence in respect of their respective claim. It is difficult to understand what further fact to be established by the parties adducing fresh evidence while parties have lead evidence to establish their case regarding period of accretion of the land in suit and there is no insufficiency of evidence for arriving at the finding and decision as regard the period of accretion of the land in suit. The plaintiffs filed the suit seeking the relief as stated hereinbefore and led evidence in support thereof. The defendants in rebuttal of the claim of the plaintiffs and in proof of their case led evidence. The Trial Court on detailed discussions of the evidence and upon consideration of the law involved in the case made decision as regard the case of the parties on merit. It is difficult for us to understand what remains for the parties to establish since no new fact was placed before the High Court Division which needs adjudication by the trial Court upon affording the parties opportunity to adduce evidence in support of the fact so placed before the appellate Court. The plaintiff did also not raise question of law mixed with fact before the appellate Court and the question so raised could only be adjudicated upon taking fresh evidence. The law is settled now that an order of remand is not well founded in law if the same is premium for the laches and negligence of one of the parties to the suit or to enable a party to fill up a lacuna in his case which in spite of the opportunity to fill up the said gap, the party did not care to take step in that regard. 

 22. In that state of the matter we find merit in the appeal.
